blocks.p: Okada took Kuga back to the grey block in a taxi. She sat with the carrier on her knees, and the cat inside it sulked like a wet king. Rei walked home along the river. The last trains had already gone. And a man with what Rei had in his hands should not be underground, packed in among other people, until he understood what he was carrying.

It was after one in the morning. The river path was empty, and the city on both sides of it had gone quiet in the way Tokyo goes quiet, never fully. A taxi crawled along the road above with its red light on, looking for a fare. Up on a bridge, a delivery scooter went by with a box of something on the back. On the far bank a single window was lit high up in a block of flats, and in it a man in a vest sat at a table eating noodles out of a cup, alone, at one in the morning, during the festival of the dead. Rei watched him until the angle of the bank took him away.

The marks settled as he walked. That was the word for it. Settled, the way mud settles in still water, the way a tenant settles into a room. It was the way something on a person becomes something inside him while he is busy thinking about other things. By the second bridge he could no longer tell the difference between reaching out with his own thin sight and reaching out with the borrowed grain. So he made himself stop reaching at all. He pushed his hands into his pockets and kept them there.

It did not help much. On the third bridge, a drunk had left an empty beer can standing on the railing. A car horn sounded and Rei flinched, and the can slid away from him along the rail and dropped into the water, though his hand was nowhere near it. Telekinesis. Force with no hand behind it, the most visible thing a practitioner can do. He stood looking at the ripples. He thought of every page in Gin's book that said people who could do that learned to hide young, the first time a cup moved at the dinner table.

blocks.cap: A streetlamp flaring as Rei passes beneath it

blocks.p: Under the expressway, a streetlamp brightened as he passed beneath it. It grew too bright, humming like a struck wire, and then went out. The vending machine beside it flickered its lights and restarted, and its little recorded voice thanked nobody. Rei walked faster. Somewhere a power log had just recorded a spike. Somewhere a security camera had just lost three seconds. That was Psychokinesis, the power over electricity and heat and sound. It did not leave a trail of footprints. It left a trail of paperwork.

By the river stairs, his scraped heel stopped stinging. He looked down at it under a lantern. The graze had closed over, pink and new. A moment later the cold came, a deep tiredness like the end of a very long day, and he had to sit on the step until his hands stopped shaking. Healing was not free. It took what it used from the one who did it. This was Psychometabolism, the path that works on the body. He had spent something of himself to mend a scratch he had not even minded.

blocks.cap: Other people's thoughts, reaching Rei uninvited

blocks.p: He sat on the step and counted, because Gin had taught him to count things. The old woman's thought by the pool. The jump along the edge of the water. The can. The lamp. The heel. Five paths that were not his, firing one after another like a house creaking at night. Six, with the Clairsentience he had always had. Every path there was. He had touched a man who had all of them lit at once, and the man's warmth had come home on his hands like flour.

Then he understood the shape of the coming month. The gifts would be useful exactly as far as they were dangerous. Every time the far shore's tools solved a problem for him, they would solve it a little more as him and a little less as something borrowed. And the Healer was in no hurry. It did not need to be. It had forty years of patience behind it. Rei had two paths, and an open wound that already, faintly, fit his palm.

Then he thought about Gin. He had not let himself do it since the concrete. Now he let himself think about Gin honestly, and not bravely. Gin was in there, leaning on the wall Rei had just touched from the far side. Gin was being worn by the thing that had wanted Rei to touch it. And here was the cruellest sum of the whole crossing. The gift in his hands was the best tool he had ever had for finding his brother. It was also the leash the far shore was using to walk him toward his brother's chair. Sitting on a river step with his fists in his pockets, he could not tell what his wanting was. Maybe it was love, the plain wish to use this gift to reach Gin. Or maybe it was the marks, already learning to want what the seat wanted.

All month he had been certain of one thing. Whatever else was true, he was the one in his own head. Now he was not certain. And that, he understood, was exactly the payment the far shore had meant to send home with him. Not a power. A doubt. The one wound a witness cannot read his way out of.

He got up and walked the rest of the way. The river bent north and west, back toward Kita. Near Ōji the paths became streets again, and the streets had lanterns. Outside one house, a family's okuribi had burned down to a few red sparks in its clay dish, and a cat sat beside it, watching the sparks, as if it had been asked to keep an eye on them. A konbini glowed on the corner, and the young clerk inside was asleep standing up, leaning on the counter with his chin in his hand. The heat had hardly dropped at all.

By the time he reached his own door, he had made the only decision the night would let him make. It was the real door, the one that locked itself, the one this whole month had begun behind. His decision was not about what to do with the gifts. It was whether to be honest that he had them.

The kitchen was dark through the glass. The kettle was cold. The chair across the table was empty in the small, ordinary way, not the loud way of the far shore. Rei stood on his own step with a stranger's tools printed into his hands. His brother's body was somewhere on the wrong side of a wall that rang like this room. He knew that whatever he did next would decide what kind of person reached Gin, when he finally reached him. The brother who went in. Or the thing the going in was making.

Things that hide what they are have a way of becoming what they hide. He had watched it happen all month, in a cardigan, across this table. So he went in and switched on the light and sat down in his own chair. He opened Gin's book to the back. At the top of a clean page, he wrote it in plain words, before he could make them gentler. I went through at Senju. I touched it. I came back with things in my hands that are not mine. I am writing this down so I can't pretend later that I didn't know. In the morning he would tell Okada, and Itsuki, and anyone else who needed to know what was standing in their kitchen. Tonight he would tell the book.

Then, because Gin's book was the only map he had, he turned back to the addendum on Font proximity. It was about what happens to a person who goes too close to the Font and gets thrown back. He had read it the night after the cold room, when it had been about other people. It listed four weights of damage. Light, Moderate, Heavy, Critical. The weight was set at the moment of being thrown out, and everything after that was just time. It read differently now.

The bleed was there. The edges of the kitchen looked doubled. Through the wall he could hear the hum of the neighbour's sleep, which he had never been able to hear before. That was Light. It would last weeks, and then the veil would close over again. Then he thought of the snake striking at nothing above the graveyard earth, and of Okada's fingers on its back. Something over there has your smell now. The line under Moderate said things contact them. He wrote Light in the margin, small. After a long moment he wrote maybe more beside it.

It should have been worse. He had stood closer to the centre than anyone in the restricted files, and he had walked home on his own feet. The reason was on the family page, the one where Gin had admitted to opening four paths in secret. At twenty-two, Gin had come back from the Threshold much less damaged than he had any right to be. And he had found the same thing in the case files of two Uedera ancestors. His guess, written very carefully, was this. A practitioner with more than one path open spreads the weight of being thrown back across all of them, so no single path takes the whole blow. Two paths. The searching one, and the nameless one under it, held flat since before Rei could read. They had shared the blow between them. Gin had hidden them from the registry and taught Rei to hold them down as a family habit. Tonight that habit had probably saved his mind.

Further down the same page, Gin had written his advice to anyone who had been thrown back. Find someone who has been there. Do not decide that the damage is permanent because of one bad week. And the fourth piece of advice, the one Gin had boxed in pencil.

Do not go back because the wanting says to. Rei put his finger on the line and held it there. Even now, with the light on and the kettle cold, he could feel the slope three hundred metres to the northeast, warm and patient. The part of him that had stood at the top of it wanted very badly to go and lie down at the bottom. He took his finger off the page. He turned to the clean sheet where he had written his confession. Below it, in the order they had come to him, he wrote down the rest of what he had carried back.

doc.title: The back of Gin's book, in Rei's hand
lines: A paper lantern at dusk with 逢魔時 on it. Ōmagatoki. The hour when you meet demons. A crest under it like an office seal. An office? Of what?
A notebook full of names written small. Ink on the second finger. He asked questions for a living. Like Gin.
Wooden bridges, swords, no wires. Old. Edo? Before Tokyo was Tokyo.
A road at evening. He walked with his shadow beside him. Did not cut it off. Did not follow it. Down the middle.
A plain chair. He sat down in it and the weight came on. He did not get up. The Duty chair. He was in it first.
要. Pivot. Keystone. The pin a fan turns on. Why did he give me this?

blocks.p: He looked at the last line for a long time. Gin had said the chair needed its old one. Gin had said the whole registered world had put him somewhere. And the man at the centre had not been able to tell Rei who he was. He could only hand him pieces, the way a person empties his pockets for someone he hopes will know what the things mean.
Rei traced the character again, slowly, pressing hard enough to dent the page. 要. It did not look like a word. It looked like something a man might once have answered to.

The window was going grey. Outside, the first crows were calling from the wires, and somewhere far off the first train of the day rattled over a bridge. Somewhere in the walls, the building's pipes knocked as the first neighbour ran a tap. Rei sat at the kitchen table where everything had started. For the first time since Gin went quiet on that Wednesday night, he was not only trying to find his brother. He was trying to remember someone else's name.
